title: Projects with uv and pyproject.toml
summary: How a Python project is set up in 2026: uv, pyproject.toml, the lock file and the virtual environment.

steps.title: One file describes the project
body: A modern Python project is described by **`pyproject.toml`**, the equivalent of a `.csproj`: name, Python version, dependencies, and tool settings (pytest, mypy, ruff all read it).
Most teams now drive this with **uv** (from Astral, the makers of ruff). It creates the virtual environment, resolves versions and writes a lock file, much faster than pip:
uv init invoice-tool          # pyproject.toml, .python-version, a sample main.py
uv add httpx                  # adds to dependencies, updates uv.lock and .venv
uv add --dev pytest mypy      # into [dependency-groups] dev
uv run pytest -q              # runs inside the project's .venv, synced first
uv sync --locked              # CI: install exactly uv.lock, fail if it is stale
`uv run` means you never "activate" anything: it always uses the project's `.venv`.

steps.prompt: You build a service that is deployed. Should `uv.lock` be committed?
options: Yes: CI and production then install exactly what you tested
Only for libraries published to PyPI
steps.explain: The lock file is what makes a build reproducible. Commit it and install with `uv sync --locked` in CI, which fails if `pyproject.toml` changed without updating the lock. (A library also commits it for its own CI; its users resolve their own versions.)

steps.title: Virtual environments, and the pip you will still meet
body: Python installs packages **into an interpreter**. A virtual environment is a private copy for one project, so two projects can need different versions. uv makes `.venv` for you; the classic way, still in many READMEs and Dockerfiles, is:
- Never `pip install` into the system Python: you break tools that depend on it (on Linux, `pip` refuses: "externally managed environment").
- `python -m pip` (not bare `pip`) guarantees the pip of the Python you mean.
- `.venv/` goes in `.gitignore`; it is rebuilt from the lock file.

Your code can read the project file too: `tomllib` (standard library since 3.11) parses TOML. Open the file in **binary** mode: `tomllib.load(open("pyproject.toml", "rb"))`, or use `tomllib.loads(text)`.

steps.title: Audit the dependencies
prompt: Security asked for a list of every package the project depends on. Write `dependency_names(pyproject_text: str) -> list[str]` that parses the text with `tomllib` and returns the **names only** (no version specifiers or extras), from `[project].dependencies` and from **every** group in `[dependency-groups]`, lower-cased, without duplicates, sorted.
A requirement string looks like `"httpx[http2]>=0.28"` or `"Typer >=0.15"` or `"rich"`. The name is everything before the first character that is not a letter, digit, `-`, `_` or `.`.
A file with no `[dependency-groups]` (or no dependencies at all) is fine: return what there is.
solution: specs.extend(s for s in group if isinstance(s, str))
names = {re.match(r"[A-Za-z0-9._-]+", s.strip()).group(0).lower() for s in specs}
template: Dojo.eq("names from project and every group", ["httpx", "mypy", "pytest", "rich", "ruff", "typer"], dependency_names(doc))
hints: `re.match(r"[A-Za-z0-9._-]+", spec.strip()).group(0)` takes the name off the front.
steps.explain: Real audits work exactly like this: read the manifest as data, not with string hacks. (`uv tree` and `pip-audit` do the full job, including transitive packages from the lock file.)
